analysis.one_liner: Bans racial profiling by federal, state, and local police and conditions federal grants on anti-profiling policies.
analysis.headline: The End Racial Profiling Act of 2005, sponsored by Sen. Feingold with 12 Democratic cosponsors, was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal for any law enforcement agent—federal, state, local, or tribal—to rely on race, ethnicity, national origin, or religion when deciding whom to stop, search, or question. People subjected to profiling could sue for court orders to stop the practice, and statistics showing disparate impact would count as initial evidence of a violation. States and cities would have to adopt anti-profiling policies, complaint procedures, and data collection to keep receiving major federal policing grants.
analysis.who_benefits: Black, Hispanic, Arab, Muslim, Sikh, and other drivers and pedestrians who are disproportionately stopped and searched would gain a federal right to challenge profiling in court and new avenues to file complaints through independent review boards. Communities generally benefit from data collection that reveals whether stops are justified—the bill's own findings cite Justice Department data showing searches of Black drivers turned up evidence only 8% of the time versus 17% for White drivers [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Minorities disproportionately stopped and searched by police

how_it_helps.text: Creates a nationwide ban on racial profiling and lets individuals injured by it sue for declaratory or injunctive relief in state or federal court, with attorney's fees available to prevailing plaintiffs [S2] [S3].

Makes statistical proof that stops and searches have a disparate impact on racial, ethnic, or religious minorities prima facie evidence of a violation, working around Supreme Court rulings that discriminatory motive alone does not invalidate a stop [S2] [S3].

Requires federal agencies to adopt anti-profiling policies, and requires state and local applicants for Byrne and Cops on the Beat grants to certify they have anti-profiling policies, independent complaint procedures or auditors, and data collection, with funds withheld for noncompliance [S2] [S3].
Mandates nationwide data collection on stops and searches broken down by race and ethnicity, with the Justice Department analyzing disparities and reporting publicly to Congress each year [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies bear the cost: new training, data collection systems, and complaint processes, independent review boards outside police control, exposure to civil suits, and possible loss of federal grant money if they do not comply. Taxpayers fund the grants and data systems the bill authorizes.
analysis.who_pays_short: Law enforcement agencies and federal grant programs

drawbacks.text: Disparate-impact statistics alone would constitute prima facie evidence of a violation, meaning a department could face legal action based on statistical patterns without proof that any officer acted with discriminatory intent [S2] [S3].

The compliance load—data collection on every stop, standardized reporting to the Justice Department, and an independent review board or auditor with full access to records—falls heaviest on small departments, which is why the bill itself reserves extra grant money for small and rural agencies [S3].

Tying Byrne and COPS grant money to certification creates a real risk that jurisdictions with strained police-community relations lose public safety funding before they can fix the underlying problems [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a documented problem—the Justice Department data cited in its own findings shows minority drivers were searched more often yet yielded contraband at lower rates than White drivers [S3]—and it deliberately pairs mandates with grant money to pay for training and cameras. The disparate-impact evidentiary standard is aggressive and would have produced contested litigation, and the administrative burden on small departments is real. The core trade, a federal right not to be stopped because of who you are in exchange for paperwork and review boards, is one most civil-rights legislation has accepted.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in December 2005, read twice, and sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before that Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Sen. Russell Feingold introduced the End Racial Profiling Act of 2005 on December 16, 2005, joined by 12 Democratic cosponsors including Sens. Obama, Kennedy, Kerry, Durbin, and Boxer [S1] [S3] [S4].

The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day; the action history shows no further action of any kind—no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action—before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S5].

The bill was introduced in the final weeks of the first session of a two-year Congress, a late start that left it dependent on the committee leadership deciding to take it up early in the second session [S5].

The bill's findings note that President George W. Bush declared in a 2001 address to Congress that 'racial profiling is wrong and we will end it in America,' but argue the resulting 2003 Justice Department guidance did not apply to state and local police, lacked an enforcement mechanism, and required no data collection [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Law enforcement agencies came out ahead: without the bill, none had to adopt anti-profiling policies, fund independent review boards, collect stop-and-search data by race, or risk losing Byrne and COPS grant money, and no one gained a court remedy for profiling.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Police agencies that avoided oversight and grant conditions

for.name: Sen. Russell Feingold
for.what_they_did: Introduced the End Racial Profiling Act of 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: 12 of 44 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Sens. Corzine, Lautenberg, Kennedy, Durbin, Kerry, Boxer, Dodd, Cantwell, Mikulski, Obama, and Stabenow.

against.name: Sen. Arlen Specter and the Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee Chairman and committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Received the referred bill and took no action on it—no hearing or committee vote—leaving it to die in committee when the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate floor and agenda, 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor; with no committee action it could not have reached a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 12 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on; the bill was referred to a Republican-chaired committee and never advanced, so the visible support and the inaction both split along party lines [S4] [S5].

industries.industry: Law enforcement agencies (federal, state, local, and tribal)
industries.note: The bill bans the practice of selecting people for stops and searches based on race, ethnicity, religion, or national origin, and requires agencies to adopt complaint procedures, independent review boards or auditors, and race-disaggregated data collection, with federal grant money withheld for noncompliance [S3]. Their financial and institutional interest in avoiding oversight and litigation ran against the public's interest in impartial policing [S2].

industries.industry: Police training, data systems, and in-car video technology vendors
industries.note: The bill authorizes grants for training programs, data collection systems, early-warning software, and in-car video cameras to help agencies eliminate profiling, creating demand for these products and services [S3].
